solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Standard refusal to meet Royal Marines

parts.note: the simplest refusal
standard abbreviation for the Royal Marines

explanation.surface: A routine refusal by someone to join up with the Royal Marines.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the usual level or benchmark, a synonym for a standard.

clue.text: Liar not, unusually, before a judge?

indicators.note: something done unusually is done out of its normal order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A defendant in the dock who is, for once, not lying.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant standing trial appears in court in front of the presiding magistrate or justice.

clue.text: I'm tough, ugly, oddly overlooked old emperor

indicators.note: overlooking the odd-placed letters leaves only the even ones, the second, fourth and so on

parts.note: the even letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A brutish old emperor boasting of being hard and ugly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mughal rulers of India were known as the Great Moguls, so a mogul is a historic emperor.

clue.text: Lady-killer, heroic, as an ovation shows

indicators.note: the phrase shows the answer, displaying it inside its own run of letters

parts.note: runs from the end of heroic through as an and into ovation

explanation.surface: A womaniser proves his heroic status by the applause he receives.
explanation.definitionFit: Giacomo Casanova was a famous seducer, and his name is used generically for a ladies' man.

clue.text: About to consume hot tea

indicators.note: to consume something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: short for circa, Latin for about
H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone about to drink a hot cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Cha, also spelt char, is an informal British word for tea, borrowed from Chinese.

clue.text: Fizzy spirit drink taken across recreation ground

indicators.note: one thing taken across another stretches over it on both sides, so it surrounds it

parts.note: a sling is a cocktail of spirit, sugar and water, as in gin sling
a park is a public ground for recreation

explanation.surface: A cocktail carried across a playing field.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is split open around the ground: S, then the ground, then LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparkling wine or water is fizzy, full of bubbles of gas.

clue.text: Vengeful female upset blokes with English sibling!

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned over, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: blokes is British slang for men
abbreviation for English
sis is short for sister

explanation.surface: An angry woman furious at some men and her English sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution who punished arrogance.

clue.text: Country house in Virginia, poorly kept

indicators.note: something kept is held within, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the US state abbreviation for Virginia
poorly means unwell

explanation.surface: A rural mansion in Virginia that has been badly maintained.
explanation.definitionFit: A villa is a large detached residence, typically in the countryside or abroad.

clue.text: Saint, disturbed at Magi revealing marks on his body?

indicators.note: disturbed letters have been knocked out of place and need rearranging

parts.note: standard abbreviation for saint
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A holy man shaken by the Wise Men showing him his wounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the saint of the surface is the 'his' whose body bears the marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmata are wounds resembling Christ's crucifixion wounds, said to appear on the bodies of some saints.

clue.text: Miss Marple's middle man

indicators.note: to miss something is to leave it out, here the letters named next

parts.note: Agatha Christie's sleuth, losing its middle two letters
the central pair of letters in the sleuth's name, the part that is missed

explanation.surface: The man at the centre of a Miss Marple mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss Marple' reads as Christie's detective, but Miss is a verb: drop the middle of Marple.
explanation.definitionFit: Male as a noun means a man or other male creature.

clue.text: Female soldier in US, going to right and left

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
abbreviation for right
abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A woman serving in the US army, marching right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl is a young female person, so the noun sense of the clue word fits.

clue.text: State of pasta when mixed with ink

indicators.note: mixing jumbles things together, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The sorry condition of a plate of pasta once squid ink is stirred in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of pasta' reads as a condition; State is the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Pakistan is a sovereign nation in South Asia, and a state is a country.

clue.text: See CID tip off killer in field?

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong or out of kilter, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; CID is the Criminal Investigation Department

explanation.surface: A tip-off to the detectives about a murderer in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The CID is the British police detective branch, which makes 'killer' look like a murderer; it is a farm chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: A pesticide kills insects and other pests on crops in agricultural land.

clue.text: Notices Charlie has long hair

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: Someone observes that Charlie has grown his hair long.
explanation.definitionFit: To clock someone is British slang for to spot or take note of them.

clue.text: Hanging that appears at end of play?

definitions.text: Hanging that appears at end of play?

parts.words: Hanging that appears at end of play?
parts.note: surface reading: an execution staged as the climax of a drama
setter's reading: a hanging is a drape, the theatre one that falls when the performance finishes

explanation.walkthrough: Hanging suggests a gallows scene in a tragedy; it is a piece of fabric hung up, the one lowered on stage at the close.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtain is a hanging drape, and the stage one comes down when a play ends.

clue.text: Fly perhaps from trendy religious faction

parts.note: in means fashionable
a sect is a religious splinter group

explanation.surface: Someone fleeing a fashionable cult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' reads as a verb, to escape; it is the noun, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fly is one kind of six-legged arthropod, hence the 'perhaps' marking an example.

clue.text: Shrouded in secrecy: an ideal murder weapon?

indicators.note: something shrouded in these words is wrapped up inside them

parts.note: runs from the end of secrecy through an into ideal

explanation.surface: Secretive and perfect, the poisoner's choice of weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyanide is a deadly poison, a classic method of killing in detective fiction.

clue.text: Capone, say, providing weapons is scary!

parts.note: Al Capone the gangster, so Al as an example name
arming is supplying with arms

explanation.surface: The prospect of Al Capone supplying guns is frightening.
explanation.definitionFit: Something alarming causes fear or worry, the same as being frightening.

clue.text: Roar coming from Irish lake that has taken a second

indicators.note: the lake word takes on a new letter in its second position, ousting the one there

parts.note: lough is the Irish word for a lake
taken as written

explanation.surface: A roar of laughter heard from a lake in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The A replaces the O as the second letter of the lake word.
explanation.definitionFit: A roar can be a loud burst of laughter, as in roars of mirth from an audience.

clue.text: Side of the hollow — a metre

indicators.note: a hollow thing is empty inside, so the middle of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written, then emptied of its middle
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for metre

explanation.surface: The side wall of a hollow measuring one metre.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is a sporting team, as in picking sides for a match.

clue.text: After Thursday, one doctor turning up behind two others?

parts.note: the calendar abbreviation for Thursday
Roman numeral one

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means flipping upward, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor arriving after Thursday, trailing two other people.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever finishes third in a race comes in behind two other competitors, hence the question mark.

clue.text: VAT applied to a brass instrument

parts.note: a vat is a large tub; capitals make it look like the tax
taken as written

explanation.surface: Value added tax being charged on a trumpet or trombone.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is printed in capitals to suggest Britain's sales tax, but it is a plain vat, a large container.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the lowest-pitched member of the brass family of the orchestra.

clue.text: One politician obeying the law: that goes without saying

parts.note: Roman numeral one
Member of Parliament
licit means lawful

explanation.surface: A law-abiding politician, which naturally goes without saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Implicit means understood though unstated, the very sense of being taken for granted.

clue.text: Mine's an untidy place on reflection!

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: a tip is a rubbish dump, British slang for a messy room

explanation.surface: Someone admitting, after thinking it over, that their room is a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' reads as a possessive; it is a noun, a coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit is a coal mine, the usual British word for a colliery.

clue.text: Most bogus calls taking one in? Tons!

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: phones is a verb meaning calls
Roman numeral one
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Fake calls coming in by the ton.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes inside the calls word just before its final S, then tons is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Phony means fake, so the superlative is the fakest of all.

clue.text: Not easy to get river pilot at first

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Finding a river pilot at the outset is hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep ideas are profound and hard to grasp, so get means understand here.
